title: Channels and select
subtitle: What blocks, what panics, what returns
focus_note: A nil channel blocks forever on send and receive. A closed channel panics on send, and a receive returns the remaining values and then the zero value with ok == false. Only the sender should close a channel.

drills.prompt: What happens when you send on a nil channel?
drills.note: Receiving from a nil channel blocks forever too. In a select, a nil channel's case is simply never ready.

drills.prompt: What happens when you send on a closed channel?
drills.note: Closing an already closed channel panics as well.

drills.prompt: What does a receive from a closed, empty channel return?
drills.note: Use v, ok := <-ch: ok is false once the channel is closed and drained.

drills.prompt: Who should close a channel: the sender or the receiver?
drills.note: Only the sender knows no more values are coming. A receiver that closes can make a sender panic.

drills.prompt: for v := ___ ch { … } keeps receiving until ch is closed.
v, ___ := <-ch  // false once ch is closed and drained
Several cases of a select are ready at once. Which one runs?
drills.note: Go picks uniformly at random among the ready cases, so no case starves.

drills.prompt: A select has a default case and no channel is ready. What happens?
drills.note: That's how you write a non-blocking send or receive.

drills.prompt: When is an unbuffered channel the better choice than a buffered one?
answers: When the sender must know the value was received: an unbuffered send completes only when a receiver takes it, so it doubles as a synchronization point.

drills.prompt: What does len(ch) return for a buffered channel?
answers: the number of elements queued in its buffer
drills.note: cap(ch) is the buffer size. Both are snapshots: another goroutine can change len right after you read it.
